title: Alamosa County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Alamosa County wells have a 100 ft median depth. Explore reported yields, shallow water levels and modeled finished-well costs of $11,000-$19,500.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Alamosa County
intro_html:
A shallow water level does not necessarily mean a shallow well. In Alamosa County, the median reported depth to standing water is 12 feet, while the median completed well depth is 100 feet. That distinction matters when pricing a lot or comparing drilling bids.

Colorado DWR records contain 9,982 county well permits, with 6,103 recorded as constructed. These records cover different uses and locations, not just household wells. Start with the county picture below, then narrow the search to neighboring wells around Alamosa, Alamosa East, Mosca or Hooper.

sections.heading: A 100-Foot Median Is a Starting Point, Not a Bid
sections.html:
Among 6,422 wells reporting depth, the median is 100 feet and the middle half runs from 60-250 feet. For budgeting, that means a bid based only on the median could miss a substantial amount of drilling. Ask the driller what nearby completion records support the proposed depth and how additional footage is priced.

The deeper end matters: the 90th percentile is 600 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 3,080 feet. Local ground is mixed sedimentary and alluvial material. Permits frequently name the Unconfined San Luis Valley Aquifer, while many aquifer entries are unnamed or broadly classified. Those labels alone cannot establish the water-bearing material beneath a particular lot.

sections.heading: Strong Reported Yields, but Not All From Household Wells
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 23.5 gpm, with the middle half spanning 15.0-400.0 gpm. That wide range reflects a county dataset that includes irrigation and stock wells alongside domestic supplies. Irrigation appears on 33% of permits and domestic or household use on 48%; these use categories can overlap.

Of the 1,816 records reporting yield, 78% report 15+ gpm, while 1% fall in the 1-5 gpm band. The reported share under 1 gpm is 0%, but that does not guarantee a productive well on an untested parcel. For a purchase, get a current pumping test and distinguish the well's physical output from the uses and pumping allowed by its permit.

sections.heading: Shallow Standing Water Does Not Show a Steady Countywide Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to water while the well is not pumping, not the depth of the drilled hole. Across 533 reported measurements, the median is 12 feet below ground and the middle half is 8-18 feet. A shallow standing level does not establish how much water the well can sustain under pumping.

Decade medians move from 5 feet in the 1970s to 12 in the 1980s, 15 in the 1990s, 12 in the 2000s, 10 in the 2010s and 13 in the 2020s. That is not a steady downward trend. These are changing groups of measurements, not a continuous record from the same wells, so they cannot establish a parcel's long-term supply outlook.

sections.heading: Permit Activity Around Alamosa, Mosca and Hooper
sections.html:
Alamosa County's permit history includes 1,723 permits issued in the 1970s and 1,645 in the 1990s. More recently, the records show 900 in the 2010s and 753 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2026. The latest decade is incomplete, so its total should not be treated as a finished comparison with earlier decades.

The most active drillers in the records are Rocky Mountain Waterworks Llc (Phythian, Donald L.) with 420, Heersink Drilling (Heersink, Scott) with 409, and Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.) with 381. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. When seeking a bid near Alamosa, Mosca or Hooper, ask about experience with nearby wells and comparable permitted uses.

sections.heading: Budget the Finished Well, Not Just the Hole
sections.html:
The drilling model for Alamosa County's mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground uses $50-$75 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $5,000-$7,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $11,000-$19,500.

Treat those figures as a planning allowance, not a parcel-specific quote. The 60-250-foot middle depth range is a reason to request clear footage pricing rather than assume every well will finish at the median. Have the written scope identify casing, grout, pump equipment, trench route, electrical work and testing. Confirm how access conditions and a different final depth would change the price before work begins.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Leave Room for Septic
sections.html:
The environmental map identifies 21 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. A mapped sampling site is not proof that a nearby household well is contaminated, and distance alone does not establish safety. Review the specific site's findings and obtain water testing appropriate to the property before relying on the supply.

Also inspect the wellhead, casing condition and surface drainage. A reported yield does not rule out seasonal supply trouble or predict the outcome of new drilling. Shallow standing water deserves attention during septic evaluation, but a well's static level is not a substitute for examining soil and groundwater conditions at the proposed septic location.

sections.heading: Before Closing on an Alamosa County Lot
sections.html:
Match the DWR permit, completion report and mapped location to the actual well serving the property. Confirm that the permitted uses cover your plans; a household-use permit should not be assumed to authorize irrigation or stock watering. For a new well, verify permit eligibility with DWR before treating water access as settled. Augmentation requirements can matter in over-appropriated basins.

Compare neighboring records within the same part of Alamosa County rather than borrowing expectations from Rio Grande County or Conejos County. Then coordinate the well location with the driveway, house, septic area and utility trench. On an existing home, review current pumping and water-quality results alongside the permit. On vacant land, make water feasibility part of the purchase decision, not an assumption left for construction.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Alamosa County?
faq.a: The median reported well depth in Alamosa County is 100 feet, and the middle half of reported depths runs from 60-250 feet. The 90th percentile is 600 feet. Use nearby completion records to refine a drilling estimate, because the county median combines different locations, aquifer conditions and well uses.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Alamosa County?
faq.a: The county cost model uses $50-$75 per foot for drilling. At the 100-foot median depth, the hole is about $5,000-$7,500, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $11,000-$19,500. Ask for a written scope and additional-footage pricing; actual depth, access and equipment requirements can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Alamosa County?
faq.a: Among 1,816 records reporting pump yield, the median is 23.5 gpm and the middle half spans 15.0-400.0 gpm. Those figures include irrigation and other uses, not just homes. A buyer should obtain a current pumping test and review the permit: reported production does not establish what uses are legally allowed.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Alamosa County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established for the individual well through testing and inspection. The map shows 21 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but those counts do not prove contamination at a property. Review relevant site information and arrange appropriate water-quality testing before buying.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Alamosa County?
faq.a: The supplied decade medians do not show a steady decline. Reported static levels range from a median of 5 feet below ground in the 1970s to 13 feet in the 2020s, with fluctuations between them. These measurements represent different groups of wells, so they cannot establish a long-term trend for an individual property.
